title: CPU scheduling
scopeHtml:
Scope: FCFS/SJF/RR, priorities, starvation and inversion, Linux CFS/EEVDF and cgroup throttling, load average, affinity and NUMA.

Scope: FCFS/SJF/RR, priorities, starvation and inversion, Linux CFS/EEVDF and cgroup throttling, load average, affinity and NUMA.

notes.title: Why scheduling exists
notes.html:
The scheduler decides which runnable task gets which CPU core, and for how long. There are almost always more runnable tasks than cores, so the OS time-slices them so fast it looks simultaneous.

Goals that conflict:

  • Throughput: finish as much work per second as possible.
  • Latency/response time: interactive tasks should react in milliseconds.
  • Fairness: nobody starves.
  • Turnaround and waiting time: batch jobs should finish soon.
  • Low overhead: the scheduler itself must be cheap (it runs on every wake-up and tick).

Preemptive schedulers can take the CPU away (timer interrupt); non-preemptive ones wait until a task yields or blocks.

Worked example. 4 cores, 12 CPU-bound threads, each needs 1 s of CPU. Ideal total: 12 / 4 = 3 s. Each thread gets 1/3 of a core, so each takes about 3 s to finish, not 1. That is why p99 latency rises as CPU utilisation nears 100%.

Industry examples. Linux CFS (2007 to 6.5) and EEVDF (6.6+), Windows multilevel feedback priorities, Android adds foreground/background cgroups and the schedutil governor for battery.

Everyday analogy. One checkout counter per core and a queue of shoppers; the rule for who goes next is the scheduler.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing scheduling as if there is one best algorithm. Every policy trades latency, throughput and fairness.
  • Forgetting that blocked tasks (waiting on I/O) are not in the run queue.

notes.title: FCFS, SJF and round robin
notes.html:
The classic textbook algorithms show the trade-offs.

FCFS (first come first served): run in arrival order, no preemption. Simple, but the convoy effect: one long job makes short ones wait.

SJF (shortest job first): run the shortest next. Provably minimises average waiting time, but needs to know job length (it does not) and starves long jobs. SRTF is its preemptive version.

Round robin (RR): each task gets a time quantum (say 10 ms), then goes to the back of the queue. Good response time and fair; if the quantum is too big it degrades to FCFS, too small and context switching dominates (quantum 1 ms with 5 microsecond switches is 0.5% overhead; 20 microseconds quantum would be 25%).

Worked example. Jobs A=24 ms, B=3 ms, C=3 ms arriving together.

  • FCFS order A,B,C: waits 0, 24, 27 = average 17 ms.
  • SJF order B,C,A: waits 0, 3, 6 = average 3 ms.
  • RR with quantum 4 ms: B finishes at 7, C at 10, A at 30; average waiting about 5.7 ms and nobody waits long for first run.
FCFS: |A.......................|B..|C..|
SJF : |B..|C..|A.......................|
RR  : |A...|B..|C..|A...|A...|A...|A...|A...|

Decision gravity. Choosing a policy is reversible in software (Linux lets you change class per task with chrt), but a general-purpose OS cannot know job length, so real systems use heuristics: run time so far, sleep history, priority.

Everyday analogy. A supermarket: a "10 items or fewer" lane is SJF; a single mixed lane is FCFS; a teacher giving every student 2 minutes in turn is round robin.

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending SJF without saying it needs a prediction and can starve.
  • Not stating how the quantum size changes behaviour.

notes.title: Priorities, starvation and aging
notes.html:
A priority scheduler always runs the highest-priority runnable task. Low-priority tasks may never run: starvation.

Fixes:

  • Aging: raise priority of waiting tasks over time.
  • Multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ): several queues; new tasks enter high; a task that uses its full quantum drops down (CPU hog), one that blocks early stays high (interactive). Periodically everything is boosted. Used in classic Unix and Windows.
  • Priority inversion: a low task holds a lock the high task needs, while a medium task preempts the low one, so the high one is blocked by the medium. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets were this. Fix: priority inheritance (the lock holder temporarily gets the waiter's priority; Linux PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT, rt_mutex).

Linux specifics:

  • Nice values -20 (greedy) to +19 (polite) for normal tasks; each step is about a 10% CPU share difference.
  • Real-time classes SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR (priority 1 to 99) always beat normal tasks. A runaway real-time loop can freeze the box; the kernel throttles with sched_rt_runtime_us (default 950000 of every 1000000 microseconds).
  • SCHED_DEADLINE for hard periodic jobs.
nice -n 10 ./batch_job          # start polite
renice -n 5 -p 4410             # adjust live
chrt -f -p 50 4410              # SCHED_FIFO priority 50 (careful)
chrt -p 4410                    # show policy

Industry examples. Audio pipelines and robotics use SCHED_FIFO; Kubernetes maps CPU requests to cgroup shares and limits to CFS quota; Android lowers background app priority via cgroups.

Everyday analogy. An airport fast lane: VIPs go first, so economy passengers must eventually be let through (aging) or they never fly.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing priority inversion with starvation.
  • Setting SCHED_FIFO for convenience on a shared server.

notes.title: Linux CFS and EEVDF
notes.html:
CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler, Linux 2.6.23 to 6.5) gives every task a fair share of CPU instead of fixed timeslices. It tracks vruntime, the weighted time a task has used. Always run the task with the smallest vruntime; the tasks sit in a red-black tree keyed by vruntime, leftmost is next (lookup O(1), insert O(log n)).

Details:

  • Higher weight (lower nice) makes vruntime grow slower, so the task runs more.
  • A target latency (about 6 ms for few tasks) is divided among runnable tasks, with a minimum granularity (about 0.75 ms). With 100 runnable tasks slices shrink to the minimum.
  • A task that slept long gets a wake-up bonus (its vruntime is placed near the minimum), so interactive tasks run promptly.
  • Separate run queue per core with load balancing between cores, aware of cache, NUMA and hyperthreads.
  • cgroup CPU control: cpu.shares/cpu.weight is proportional sharing; cpu.cfs_quota_us / cpu.max is a hard cap. A container limited to 2 CPUs gets 200 ms of CPU per 100 ms window; once spent, all its threads are throttled until the next window. Symptom: latency spikes with low average CPU; metric container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total or nr_throttled in cpu.stat.

EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) replaced CFS in Linux 6.6 (2023). It adds a per-task deadline derived from requested slice, giving better latency fairness with fewer heuristics. The idea (tasks get a fair share and the one with the earliest deadline among eligible runs) is what to remember; confirm tunables for your kernel version.

cat /proc/sched_debug | head -40          # older kernels; newer: /sys/kernel/debug/sched/
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<grp>/cpu.stat         # nr_throttled, throttled_usec

Production incident. A Java service in Kubernetes with limits.cpu: 2 on a 64-core node shows p99 jumps every 100 ms. The JVM sees 64 cores, spawns 64 GC threads, burns the quota in 30 ms, then is throttled for 70 ms. Fixes: raise or remove the CPU limit, set -XX:ActiveProcessorCount or use a container-aware JVM (JDK 10+ is), reduce thread counts.

Everyday analogy. Splitting a pizza so everybody ends up with equal slices over time; whoever has had least eats next.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying CFS uses a fixed time quantum. It uses weighted fair share.
  • Treating CPU limits as harmless; throttling is a top cause of tail latency in containers.

notes.title: Load average and run queues
notes.html:
Load average is the average number of tasks that are runnable or in uninterruptible sleep (D), over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. It is not CPU percent.

$ uptime
 10:05:01 up 12 days,  load average: 8.10, 6.25, 3.02
$ nproc
8

Reading it: compare to core count. On 8 cores, a load of 8 means roughly full; 16 means each core has a waiting task; the trend (1 min above 15 min) says rising. Linux counts D tasks too, so a stuck disk can give load 50 with idle CPUs. (Many other Unixes count only runnable tasks.)

To tell the cause apart:

$ vmstat 1 3
procs -----memory---- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
12  0      0 812344 120344 4123400    0    0     8    20 5100 9000 85 10  3  2  0
  • r = runnable tasks (CPU pressure when above cores), b = blocked in D (I/O pressure), us/sy/id/wa as before, cs context switches.
  • Newer kernels (4.20+) expose PSI (pressure stall information): cat /proc/pressure/cpu, /proc/pressure/io, /proc/pressure/memory give "some avg10=…" percentages of time tasks were stalled. This is a better saturation signal than load average; Facebook's oomd uses it.
top -H -p <pid>        # per-thread CPU
mpstat -P ALL 1        # per-core: one core at 100% means single-thread bottleneck
pidstat -u -t 1        # per-thread user/system CPU

Decision flow:

Worked example. Load 40 on 8 cores, us 5%, wa 90%, b 38: not a CPU problem; 38 tasks wait on a slow EBS volume. Adding cores changes nothing; check iostat -x 1 (await, %util).

Everyday analogy. Number of people standing at a doctor's door compared with the number of doctors. It does not say whether they wait for a doctor or for an X-ray.

Common interview traps.

  • Equating load 1.0 with 100% CPU on multicore.
  • Ignoring D-state tasks when diagnosing high load.
  • Using load average alone with no r/b/PSI breakdown.

notes.title: Multicore: affinity, NUMA and balancing
notes.html:
With many cores the scheduler also decides where a task runs, not just when. Moving a task to another core loses its warm L1/L2 cache; moving across a NUMA node makes its memory slower (remote access is roughly 1.5x to 2x the latency).

Concepts:

  • Per-core run queues plus periodic and idle load balancing. Balance too eagerly and caches thrash; too lazily and one core is busy while another idles.
  • CPU affinity: pin a task to chosen cores (taskset -c 0-3 ./app, sched_setaffinity). Used for latency-sensitive services and to keep interrupts apart from workers.
  • NUMA: numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./db; check numastat. Databases often interleave memory (numactl --interleave=all) to avoid one node filling up and swapping.
  • Hyperthreads share one core's execution units: two threads get roughly 1.2x to 1.3x one thread's throughput, not 2x. Cloud "vCPU" is usually a hyperthread.
  • isolcpus / cpuset reserve cores for a special workload (trading, packet processing).
lscpu | grep -E 'NUMA|Thread|Core'
taskset -cp 4410
perf stat -e cpu-migrations,context-switches -p 4410 -- sleep 10

Industry examples. ScyllaDB shards one thread per core with its own memory; Redis recommends pinning the main thread away from persistence child processes; Kubernetes static CPU manager policy gives Guaranteed pods exclusive cores.

Everyday analogy. A chef who keeps their tools at their own station. Moving them to another kitchen means fetching tools all over again.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming vCPU = physical core.
  • Pinning threads and forgetting that pinned cores can't be rebalanced if neighbours are busy.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Scheduling = choosing which runnable task runs on which core; goals conflict (latency, throughput, fairness).
  • FCFS has the convoy effect, SJF is optimal for average wait but needs predictions and starves, round robin trades quantum size against switching overhead.
  • Priorities cause starvation (fix with aging/MLFQ) and priority inversion (fix with priority inheritance). Linux has nice, real-time classes and deadline.
  • CFS runs the smallest vruntime from a red-black tree; EEVDF (6.6+) adds deadlines. cgroup quotas cause throttling, a classic container tail-latency source.
  • Load average counts runnable plus D tasks; read it with core count, vmstat r/b, and PSI.
  • Affinity, NUMA, hyperthreads and balancing govern where tasks run; cache warmth matters.

questions.promptHtml: What does the CPU scheduler do, what goals conflict, and what is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline understanding of the problem scheduling solves, and the instinct that every policy is a trade-off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The scheduler decides which runnable task gets which core and for how long. There are nearly always more runnable tasks than cores, so it time-slices them. Goals conflict: throughput, low latency for interactive tasks, fairness, short turnaround for batch work, and low scheduler overhead. A preemptive scheduler can take the CPU away using the timer interrupt; a non-preemptive one waits until the task yields or blocks. Blocked tasks are not in the run queue.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
New task -> Run queue -> Scheduler -> CPU core -> (slice ends) -> Run queue
                                         |-> blocks on I/O -> wait queue -> wake -> Run queue

Worked example: 4 cores, 12 CPU-bound threads, each needs 1 s of CPU. Total work 12 s on 4 cores is 3 s. Every thread gets a third of a core, so each finishes at about 3 s, not 1 s. This is why p99 latency rises sharply as utilisation approaches 100%.

Linux: CFS (2.6.23 to 6.5), EEVDF (6.6+). Windows uses multilevel feedback priorities. Android adds foreground/background cgroups.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Describing one "best" algorithm.
  • Forgetting that blocked tasks are not runnable.
  • Treating scheduler overhead as zero (it runs on every wakeup and tick).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can an infinite loop not freeze a Linux box? -> The timer tick triggers preemption.
  2. What is turnaround vs response time? -> Turnaround is submission to completion; response is submission to first run.
  3. Why does latency explode near full utilisation? -> Queueing: waiting time grows non-linearly (roughly 1/(1-rho)) as load approaches capacity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists algorithms. Senior frames it as latency vs throughput vs fairness and links it to tail latency in production.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service at 90% CPU "looked fine" until traffic rose 5%; p99 tripled because run-queue wait grew non-linearly.

questions.promptHtml: Compare FCFS, SJF and round robin. Three jobs arrive together with lengths 24 ms, 3 ms and 3 ms; compute the average waiting time for each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you can both reason about trade-offs and do the arithmetic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: FCFS runs in arrival order with no preemption: simple, but the convoy effect makes short jobs wait behind a long one. SJF runs the shortest next: provably minimal average wait, but it needs job lengths (which we do not know) and starves long jobs. Round robin gives each task a quantum then moves it to the back: fair with good response time, but too large a quantum degrades to FCFS and too small drowns in context switches. For the example: FCFS (A,B,C) average wait is (0+24+27)/3 = 17 ms; SJF (B,C,A) is (0+3+6)/3 = 3 ms; RR with quantum 4 ms is about 5.7 ms.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
FCFS: |A.......................|B..|C..|
SJF : |B..|C..|A.......................|
RR  : |A...|B..|C..|A...|A...|A...|A...|A...|

RR with quantum 4: A runs 0-4, B 4-7 (done), C 7-10 (done), A 10-30. Waits: A = 6 (waited while B and C ran, 3+3), B = 4, C = 7 -> average (6+4+7)/3 = 5.67 ms.

Quantum trade-off: 1 ms with 5 microsecond switches is 0.5% overhead; 20 microsecond quantum would be 25%. General-purpose OSes cannot know job length, so they use heuristics: CPU time used so far, sleep history, priority. SRTF is the preemptive version of SJF.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Recommending SJF without noting it needs prediction and starves.
  • Ignoring how quantum size changes RR behaviour.
  • Computing waiting time as completion time (turnaround).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is SJF optimal for average wait? -> Swapping a longer job ahead of a shorter one always increases total waiting.
  2. How do real schedulers estimate job length? -> Exponential averaging of previous bursts, or MLFQ demotion of CPU hogs.
  3. How does quantum choice affect interactive tasks? -> Smaller quantum improves response time but raises switch overhead and cache misses.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average recites definitions. Senior does the numbers, ties to the convoy effect (one slow request blocking a single-threaded queue) and quantum versus overhead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A single-threaded worker queue processing mixed 1 ms and 5 s jobs had p99 dominated by the convoy effect; separating queues by job size fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What does load average actually measure, and how do you tell whether high load means a CPU problem or an I/O problem?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Load average is misread constantly; seniors know it includes D tasks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Load average is the exponentially weighted average, over 1, 5 and 15 minutes, of tasks that are runnable or in uninterruptible sleep. It is not CPU percent. Compare it to core count: load 8 on 8 cores is roughly full. On Linux it includes D tasks, so a hung disk can give load 50 with idle CPUs. To split the cause I look at vmstat: r (runnable) high means CPU pressure, b (blocked in D) high means I/O pressure. Newer kernels also give PSI in /proc/pressure/.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
$ uptime
 load average: 8.10, 6.25, 3.02     (rising: 1-min above 15-min)
$ vmstat 1 3
 r  b  swpd free ... us sy id wa st
12  0  ...             85 10  3  2  0     -> CPU bound (r>cores)
 2 38  ...              5  2  3 90  0     -> I/O bound (b high)

Decision flow: high load -> check r and b -> r high: profile or scale out; b high: iostat -x 1 (await, %util). PSI some avg10 percentages are a better saturation signal than load average. mpstat -P ALL 1 shows if one core is pegged (single-thread bottleneck). Many other Unixes count only runnable tasks.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating load 1.0 with 100% CPU on multicore.
  • Ignoring D tasks.
  • Looking at load without r, b or PSI.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Load is 16 on 16 cores. Is that bad? -> About fully used with no queueing; look at the trend and latency.
  2. Why exponential averaging? -> Cheap to compute and smooths spikes; so 15-minute value lags.
  3. What is PSI? -> Pressure stall information: the share of time tasks were stalled on CPU, I/O or memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average says "load above cores is bad". Senior separates CPU from I/O pressure, knows D is included, and uses PSI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A page for "CPU saturation" at load 40 was actually a slow EBS volume; adding cores did nothing.

questions.contextHtml:
At 03:10 an on-call page says "load average 40 on 8 cores, API latency 30 s". Output:

$ uptime
 03:12:01 up 41 days, load average: 41.2, 38.7, 22.5
$ top -bn1 | head -4
%Cpu(s):  4.0 us,  2.0 sy,  0.0 ni,  4.0 id, 90.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
$ vmstat 1 3
 r  b   swpd   free   ...   us sy id wa
 1 39      0 2200000 ...    4  2  4 90
$ ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:22,cmd | awk '$2 ~ /^D/' | head -3
 6101 D    nfs_wait_bit_killable  /usr/bin/exporter
 6240 D    jbd2_log_wait_commit   postgres: writer
$ iostat -x 1 2 | grep nvme1n1
nvme1n1  ... await 4800.00  %util 100.0

The team is about to double the instance size and wants kill -9 on the stuck processes.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CPU overload, scale up." CPU is 90% waiting, not busy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed (deploy, volume event, backup job)? Is the volume network-attached (EBS/NFS)? Are cloud provider health events open? Is a snapshot or fstrim running?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load: take the node out of rotation and stop non-essential writers (backups, exporters). Fail over the database if a replica exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the storage volume is stalled or throttled (await 4.8 s, %util 100); (b) NFS server hang; (c) filesystem journal commit blocked; (d) CPU (ruled out: r is 1, us 4%).
  4. How I'd verify each: iostat -x 1, cat /proc/pressure/io, dmesg -T | tail for I/O errors or timeouts, cloud volume metrics (burst balance, queue length), cat /proc/PID/stack.
  5. Root cause (mechanism): Linux counts D tasks in load average. 39 tasks blocked on disk produce load 40 while CPUs are idle. Signals do not interrupt D, so kill -9 does nothing.
  6. Fix: Short-term: restore or replace the volume, or fail over; remove the throttling workload. Long-term: provision IOPS, isolate backup traffic, alert on await and PSI io.
  7. Prevention: Alert on /proc/pressure/io and iostat await, not load alone; runbook that distinguishes r from b.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not resize the instance (wrong resource). Not force-reboot without first checking replication state; unflushed writes may be lost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did load rise slowly (22 to 41)? -> It is an exponential average; instantaneous b jumped first.
  • Can kill -9 ever clear D? -> Only when the kernel call returns (I/O completes or times out); for NFS use soft or intr mounts if appropriate.
  • Why is free memory fine? -> Not a memory issue; no swap in/out.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A burst-balance exhausted volume produced precisely this picture every Monday after the weekly job; moving to provisioned IOPS ended the pages.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales CPU.
  • Hire: reads wa/b/iostat, identifies storage.
  • Strong hire: explains D in load, uses PSI, plans failover and alerting changes.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between starvation and priority inversion, and how are each solved?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These two get confused. A good answer shows concurrency and scheduling knowledge together.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Starvation: a strict priority scheduler always runs higher-priority tasks, so a low-priority one may never run. Fixes: aging (raise priority of waiting tasks) or a multilevel feedback queue. Priority inversion: a low-priority task holds a lock the high-priority task needs, and a medium-priority task preempts the low one, so the high task is blocked by the medium one. Fix: priority inheritance, where the lock holder temporarily runs at the waiter's priority. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets were this.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Inversion:  High waits for lock held by Low
            Medium runs (preempts Low) -> Low cannot release -> High stuck behind Medium
Fix:        Low inherits High's priority -> runs -> releases lock -> High proceeds
  • MLFQ: new tasks enter the top queue; using a full quantum drops a task (CPU hog), blocking early keeps it high (interactive); periodic boost prevents starvation.
  • Linux: nice -20 to +19 for normal tasks (about 10% share per step); real-time SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_RR priorities 1-99 always beat normal tasks; SCHED_DEADLINE. A runaway real-time loop can freeze a box, so the kernel throttles with sched_rt_runtime_us (default 950000 of every 1000000).
  • PI mutexes: pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT), kernel rt_mutex.
nice -n 10 ./batch_job
renice -n 5 -p 4410
chrt -p 4410            # show policy

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing the two: starvation is about the scheduler policy, inversion needs a lock.
  • Assuming CFS has strict priorities (it uses weights).
  • Setting SCHED_FIFO for convenience on shared servers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does priority inheritance work? -> The kernel boosts the holder to the highest waiter's priority until it releases.
  2. Alternative to inheritance? -> Priority ceiling protocol, or avoid sharing locks across priorities.
  3. Does inversion happen with CFS? -> Not as classic inversion, but a low-weight task holding a lock can still delay a high-weight one; mutexes in user space (futex) use no inheritance unless requested.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average defines both. Senior names the mechanisms (aging, MLFQ, PI mutex), real-time throttling, and when RT classes are dangerous.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An audio daemon in SCHED_FIFO starved the logging thread of a lower class, which held a lock the daemon needed; PI mutexes fixed the stall.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java service on Kubernetes (requests.cpu: 1, limits.cpu: 2) runs on 64-core nodes. Average CPU is 25% of the limit but p99 spikes to 800 ms every few seconds; p50 is 15 ms. No GC pauses beyond 20 ms. Metrics:

$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat
usage_usec 91233444000
nr_periods 640000
nr_throttled 210000
throttled_usec 41220000000
$ jcmd 1 VM.info | grep -i 'active_processor'
active_processor_count: 64

A teammate wants to double the pod's memory since "it must be GC".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add memory" or "average CPU is low, so it's not CPU". Averages hide throttling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: cgroup v1 or v2? Is the JVM container-aware (JDK 10+ is) and what does it detect? How many GC and compiler threads run? Are other limits set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise or remove the CPU limit (keep the request), or set -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) CFS quota exhausted early in each 100 ms window by many threads, then all threads stopped until the next period; (b) GC threads (64) burn quota in bursts; (c) CPU steal; (d) GC pauses (ruled out).
  4. How I'd verify each: nr_throttled / nr_periods = 33% of periods throttled; throttled_usec; Prometheus container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total; thread counts by name via jstack; -Xlog:gc.
  5. Root cause: limits.cpu: 2 means 200 ms CPU time per 100 ms period across all threads. A JVM that sizes pools by 64 visible cores runs up to 64 threads in parallel and spends 200 ms of quota in about 3 ms to 30 ms of wall time, then every thread is frozen until the period ends. Average CPU stays low, tail latency spikes.
  6. Fix: Short-term: set ActiveProcessorCount, cap GC/parallel threads, raise the limit to 4. Long-term: use requests without CPU limits for latency-critical services (and rely on cpu.weight), or CPU manager static policy for exclusive cores.
  7. Prevention: Alert on throttled-period ratio above a few percent; load test with the production limits; set thread pools from container CPU count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Removing limits risks noisy-neighbour contention; guaranteed pods with integer CPUs cost more. Not chase GC tuning.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does a limit of 2 CPUs not mean "2 cores"? -> It is a time budget, not a core assignment.
  • cpuset vs quota? -> cpuset pins to specific cores (no throttling), quota caps total time.
  • Does cgroup v2 change anything? -> cpu.max replaces cfs_quota_us; same throttling idea.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet-wide p99 improvement of 60% came from removing CPU limits on latency services and instead keeping requests accurate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames GC or memory.
  • Hire: finds throttling in cpu.stat and fixes limit/thread count.
  • Strong hire: explains quota windows, JVM core detection, and the limits vs requests policy.

questions.promptHtml: How does Linux's CFS decide which task runs next, and what changed with EEVDF?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests real Linux scheduler knowledge beyond textbook round robin.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CFS gives each task a fair share of CPU instead of a fixed quantum. It tracks vruntime, the weighted CPU time a task has consumed, keeps runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by it, and always runs the leftmost (smallest vruntime). Lower nice means a higher weight, so vruntime grows slower and the task runs more. Tasks that slept get placed near the minimum so interactive tasks run promptly. EEVDF (Linux 6.6) keeps the fair share but adds per-task virtual deadlines derived from requested slice length: among eligible tasks, the one with the earliest deadline runs, which improves latency fairness with fewer heuristics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Runnable tasks -> rb-tree by vruntime -> leftmost runs -> vruntime += delta * (1024/weight) -> reinsert
  • Target latency (about 6 ms for few tasks) divided among runnable tasks, minimum granularity (about 0.75 ms), so with 100 tasks slices shrink to the minimum (values vary; verify on your kernel).
  • Per-core run queues with load balancing aware of caches, NUMA and hyperthreads.
  • cgroups: cpu.weight (proportional) and cpu.max (hard cap, causing throttling).
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<grp>/cpu.stat           # nr_throttled, throttled_usec
cat /proc/sched_debug | head -40            # older kernels; newer: /sys/kernel/debug/sched/

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "CFS uses a fixed time quantum."
  • Treating CPU limits as harmless.
  • Quoting CFS tunables as present on 6.6+ kernels (EEVDF changed them; verify).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Complexity? -> Pick next O(1) (cached leftmost), insert O(log n).
  2. Why give a waking task a vruntime near the minimum? -> So a task that slept does not arrive with a huge credit and monopolise the CPU, but still gets to run soon.
  3. What does nice 0 vs nice 10 mean? -> Roughly 1024 vs 110 weight, so nice 0 gets about 9x more CPU when competing (verify the weight table).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it's fair". Senior: vruntime, weights, rb-tree, cgroup quota vs weight, and the EEVDF change and its latency motivation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A kernel upgrade to 6.6 shifted latency characteristics of a mixed batch/interactive host; teams re-ran benchmarks rather than assuming old tunables.

questions.contextHtml:
You own a custom job runner (single worker pool of 4 threads, FIFO queue). Job mix: 95% are 5 ms jobs, 5% are 3 s report jobs. Users complain that simple lookups sometimes take 6+ seconds. Queue metrics at peak:

arrival: 20 jobs/s     workers: 4    queue depth p99: 55
wait time p50: 40 ms   p99: 6,200 ms

Mean service time is 0.95 x 5 ms + 0.05 x 3000 ms, about 155 ms. Worker utilisation at peak is about 78% (20 jobs/s x 155 ms = 3.1 of 4 workers), so the long jobs dominate the load. Someone proposes making the pool bigger; another suggests time-slicing the reports.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how would you redesign scheduling?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more workers" without seeing the convoy effect.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can reports be split or paused? Do we know job class at submit time? What latency targets per class? Are jobs CPU-bound?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reserve 1 of the 4 workers for short jobs only so lookups never queue behind a report.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) FCFS convoy: short jobs wait behind a 3 s job on each worker; (b) utilisation near saturation inflates queues; (c) too few workers (secondary).
  4. How I'd verify each: Wait time split by job class; queue depth by class; worker busy time; replay a trace in a simple simulator.
  5. Root cause: FCFS with heavy-tailed service times: one long job holds a worker while many short ones accumulate. Mean wait is dominated by the long-job variance, not average load.
  6. Fix: Short-term: separate queues/pools by class (a poor man's SJF using known class), priority to short jobs with aging so reports cannot starve. Long-term: chunk reports into 100 ms units (cooperative quantum) so shorter jobs interleave (round robin by chunk), and add admission control.
  7. Prevention: Per-class SLOs and queue-wait alerts, load shedding for reports at peak, load tests with the real mix.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pure SJF starves reports; reserving workers wastes capacity when no short jobs arrive (use work stealing in one direction only). Not just add threads: it hides the convoy, then CPU contention returns.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What quantum would you pick for report chunks? -> Large relative to switch cost (here, tens of ms) and small relative to the short job SLO.
  • Job length unknown at submit? -> Use MLFQ: new jobs start at high priority, demote after consuming a chunk.
  • Why not preemptive kill and restart of reports? -> Wasted work; checkpoints are better.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An email-sending queue with one slow template caused hourly delivery spikes until the team split queues by expected duration.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales workers.
  • Hire: identifies convoy, separates short and long jobs.
  • Strong hire: combines class queues, chunking, aging and admission control, justified by numbers.

questions.promptHtml: On a multicore server, what do CPU affinity, NUMA and hyperthreading mean for scheduling and performance?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that placement matters, not just timing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With many cores the scheduler also decides where a task runs. Moving a task loses warm L1/L2 cache; on a multi-socket NUMA machine, accessing memory attached to another node costs roughly 1.5x to 2x the latency. Affinity (taskset, sched_setaffinity) pins tasks to cores to keep caches warm or keep interrupts separate. Hyperthreads share one core's execution units, so two threads give about 1.2x to 1.3x throughput, not 2x, and a cloud vCPU is usually one hyperthread. Load balancing must trade idle cores against cache thrash.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Thread -> Core 3 -> L2 cache -> Local NUMA memory (fast)
Thread -> Core on node 1 -> memory on node 0 (remote, slower)
lscpu | grep -E 'NUMA|Thread|Core'
taskset -c 0-3 ./app            # pin to cores 0-3
numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./db
numactl --interleave=all ./db   # spread memory across nodes
numastat -p <pid>
perf stat -e cpu-migrations,context-switches -p <pid> -- sleep 10

Tools: isolcpus/cpuset reserve cores; Kubernetes static CPU manager gives Guaranteed pods exclusive cores. ScyllaDB shards one thread per core with its own memory.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming vCPU = physical core.
  • Pinning threads then ignoring that pinned cores cannot be rebalanced.
  • Ignoring NUMA effects when a database allocates all memory on one node.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When would you pin? -> Latency-critical services, packet processing, or to isolate interrupts from workers.
  2. Why interleave memory for databases? -> To prevent one node filling and forcing allocation on remote nodes or swapping.
  3. How do you spot cross-node traffic? -> numastat numa_miss and other_node counters, perf stat LLC/remote accesses.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average knows taskset. Senior reasons about cache warmth, NUMA locality, hyperthread capacity, and the downside of pinning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A database on a two-socket host with all memory bound to node 0 swapped while node 1 had free RAM until numactl --interleave=all was used.

questions.contextHtml:
An industrial controller (Linux, PREEMPT_RT not enabled) runs a 1 kHz control loop (SCHED_FIFO priority 80), a telemetry uploader (nice 0, normal), and a logger thread (SCHED_FIFO priority 20) sharing a std::mutex protecting a ring buffer that the control loop writes to. Occasionally the control loop misses its 1 ms deadline by 40 to 200 ms. A trace excerpt:

control-loop  [prio 80]  blocked on mutex 0x5e10 held by logger
logger        [prio 20]  runnable, waiting for CPU
metrics-agent [prio 50]  running 120 ms (SCHED_FIFO busy loop)

CPU usage is 35% overall. Someone says "just raise the logger's priority to 99".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise priorities" which creates new inversions and starvation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the mutex needed in the control loop? Who runs at prio 50? What is the worst allowed latency? Is sched_rt_runtime_us default?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the metrics agent not real-time (or lower it below 20), and cap its runtime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) classic priority inversion: high (80) waits for low (20) which is preempted by medium (50); (b) logger holding the lock across a slow call (disk write); (c) interrupts or SMIs (not indicated by the trace).
  4. How I'd verify each: ftrace/trace-cmd record -e sched_switch -e sched_wakeup, perf sched latency; check the mutex attributes (PTHREAD_PRIO_NONE by default); measure lock hold times.
  5. Root cause: While the high task blocks on the lock, the medium task keeps the CPU, so the low-priority holder cannot run to release it. The high task effectively inherits the medium's runtime, unbounded.
  6. Fix: Short-term: use a PI mutex (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT). Better: remove the lock from the control loop entirely, use a lock-free single-producer ring buffer, and let the logger drain it.
pthread_mutexattr_t a; pthread_mutexattr_init(&a);
pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(&a, PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT);
pthread_mutex_init(&m, &a);
  1. Prevention: Priority assignment document, ban shared locks between RT priorities, worst-case latency tests (cyclictest), review of every RT thread's loop for busy-waiting.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Priority ceiling/inheritance adds overhead and complexity; lock-free queues need careful design. Not set everything to 99, which makes ordering meaningless and starves kernel threads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did Mars Pathfinder resets happen? -> Same pattern; a watchdog reset the computer when a bus task was blocked by a medium-priority task; enabling inheritance fixed it.
  • Could sched_rt_runtime_us mask it? -> It throttles RT groups at 95% per second but does not fix inversion.
  • Does Linux CFS have inversion? -> Weights reduce but cannot eliminate lock-holder delays.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A robotics team found that 98% of missed deadlines in a month came from one logging mutex; moving to a lock-free queue removed all of them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises priority numbers.
  • Hire: identifies inversion and uses priority inheritance.
  • Strong hire: eliminates the lock from the hot path, validates with ftrace/cyclictest, and sets team rules.

questions.contextHtml:
A 2-socket server (2 x 24 cores, 256 GB, 128 GB per node) hosts a single large MySQL-style database with a 180 GB buffer pool. After a restart, queries are 40% slower than before and kswapd is active even though free -g shows plenty of memory overall:

$ numastat -m | egrep 'MemFree|MemUsed'
                    Node 0    Node 1
MemFree                 1200    118000
MemUsed               126800     10000
$ vmstat 1
 si  so
 450 1900
$ numactl --hardware | grep size
node 0 size: 131072 MB   node 1 size: 131072 MB

The service was started under numactl --cpunodebind=0, copied from an old runbook for a smaller host. The team wants to add swap or lower innodb_buffer_pool_size.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add swap" or "reduce the buffer pool". Both treat the symptom.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in start-up scripts? Is vm.zone_reclaim_mode set? Is automatic NUMA balancing on? What is the memory policy of the process?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If the database can restart safely, restart with numactl --interleave=all (or no binding). Avoid swapping by disabling zone_reclaim_mode.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the process is bound to node 0, so memory is allocated from node 0 which has 128 GB, not enough for 180 GB, so reclaim and swap happen while node 1 is nearly empty; (b) zone reclaim aggressively reclaims local pages; (c) real memory shortage (ruled out by node 1 free 118 GB).
  4. How I'd verify each: numastat -p $(pidof mysqld); cat /proc/<pid>/numa_maps | head; sysctl vm.zone_reclaim_mode; cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep Cpus_allowed_list.
  5. Root cause: The bind restricted CPUs and memory to one node. The workload's working set is larger than a node, so the kernel swaps or reclaims within node 0 and remote access penalty applies to what remains. Total free memory is irrelevant to a single-node policy.
  6. Fix: Short-term: restart without the node bind, using numactl --interleave=all. Long-term: allow both nodes, size buffer pool with NUMA in mind, pin interrupts and threads thoughtfully, consider one instance per node if the workload can be partitioned.
numactl --interleave=all /usr/sbin/mysqld --defaults-file=/etc/my.cnf
sysctl -w vm.zone_reclaim_mode=0
  1. Prevention: Remove copied runbook flags, test config changes on matching hardware, alert on numa_miss and swap activity.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Interleave gives average latency across nodes rather than best local latency; per-node instances give locality at the cost of operational complexity. Not just add swap: it will thrash.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would hugepages help? -> They reduce TLB misses but need NUMA-aware reservation.
  • How do you detect remote memory access? -> perf stat remote DRAM events (CPU specific), numastat other_node.
  • Is interleave always right for DBs? -> Commonly recommended for large single-instance DBs; verify with benchmarks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "tuned" config copied from a one-socket host halved throughput on a two-socket host until someone looked at numastat.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds swap or lowers the pool.
  • Hire: spots node binding and fixes with interleave.
  • Strong hire: verifies with numastat/numa_maps, addresses zone reclaim and runbook hygiene.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "The nightly analytics batch must not slow down the checkout API on the same 32-core host, but it also must finish before 06:00." Today the batch (24 threads) starts at 01:00 and checkout p99 goes from 80 ms to 400 ms. Containers are used (cgroup v2). Batch needs about 20 core-hours; there are 5 hours available. Checkout peaks at about 6 cores.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and how do you configure this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just nice the batch" or "move it to another machine" with no analysis of the requirements.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "not slow down" mean numerically (p99 +10%)? Is the batch CPU-only or I/O and cache heavy (shared L3, memory bandwidth)? Can it be paused/resumed? Is the host shared in the cloud (steal)? Is a separate node an option cost-wise?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start the batch with a low weight (cpu.weight 10 vs 100 for checkout) and a thread cap of 12.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) CPU contention: 24 batch threads + checkout compete; (b) shared cache/memory bandwidth contention (not fixed by weights); (c) I/O contention.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure checkout p99 under batch with perf stat, mpstat, pidstat, iostat; check LLC misses; run the batch at several thread counts.
  5. Root cause of the conflict: Weights give proportional shares only under contention and do not guarantee latency; fair scheduling still lets batch threads run ahead of a waking API thread by up to a slice. A hard quota would cap batch but can throttle it unnecessarily.
  6. Fix: Layered: (1) cpu.weight low for batch plus SCHED_BATCH or SCHED_IDLE policy so wakeups of API threads preempt it; (2) cpuset: give checkout 8 dedicated cores and the batch the remaining 24 (batch needs 4 cores average over 5 h, so 8 is plenty); (3) cpu.max as a safety cap; (4) memory/IO controls (io.weight, memory.high).
systemctl set-property batch.slice CPUWeight=10 AllowedCPUs=8-31
chrt --idle -p 0 $BATCH_PID
  1. Prevention: Dashboards for checkout p99 vs batch progress; alerts when the batch is behind schedule; periodic review of required cores.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dedicated cores lower checkout interference but lose flexibility; SCHED_IDLE can starve the batch if the host is busy (set a deadline alert). Not rely on nice alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if latency still degrades? -> Shared L3/memory bandwidth: use Intel RDT/cache partitioning or a separate host.
  • Batch needs to finish by 06:00 but is starved? -> Raise weight near the deadline or add cores progressively.
  • Quota vs weight? -> Quota = hard ceiling (can throttle), weight = relative share (work conserving).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving a batch to cpuset-isolated cores cut checkout p99 inflation from 5x to 8%; the remaining gap came from memory bandwidth.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: uses nice only.
  • Hire: asks for numeric targets and uses cgroup weights/cpuset.
  • Strong hire: separates CPU from cache/IO interference, compares weight vs quota vs pinning, and plans deadline monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
A recommendation API has 12 pods at 8 cores each. At 4,000 rps overall CPU is 55% and p99 is 120 ms. Marketing plans a campaign for 10x traffic. Capacity plan from the team: "CPU is 55% at 4k, so 100% at about 7.3k; we need about 5.5x more capacity for 40k rps, plus a safety margin, so 80 pods". Load test at 6,500 rps on the current cluster:

rps    cpu%   p50    p99
4000   55     22ms   120ms
5000   69     25ms   180ms
6000   83     31ms   520ms
6500   90     40ms   2100ms

The service is a CPU-bound request handler with a 2 s client timeout.
questions.promptHtml: Is 80 pods right? How would you plan capacity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Linear extrapolation to 100% CPU.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What p99 target? Is traffic bursty? How fast can we autoscale? Are pods CPU-limited (throttling)? What is the request-size variance?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-scale before the campaign and enable autoscaling based on CPU plus latency or queue depth, not CPU alone.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The knee is around 70 to 75% CPU: beyond that, run-queue wait grows non-linearly (queueing theory: wait grows like rho/(1-rho)); thread contention, GC, and cache effects add to it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Extend the load test to find the knee; watch vmstat r vs cores, PSI cpu some, run-queue latency (runqlat from bcc), GC logs, throttling counters.
  5. Root cause of the wrong plan: CPU percent is utilisation, not latency. Run-queue delay depends on how many runnable tasks per core; near saturation queues build, so p99 explodes well before 100%.
  6. Fix: Plan to run at about 60 to 65% target utilisation at peak, which the data supports. At 40k rps: per-pod capacity at 65% is roughly 4,000 rps / 12 pods x (65/55) ≈ 393 rps/pod, giving about 102 pods. Add buffer for failure of one zone (N+1) and burst. Validate with a load test at the target scale, not extrapolation.
  7. Prevention: SLO-based autoscaling (HPA on p99 or queue depth), regular capacity tests, load shedding at the edge.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lower utilisation costs money; running hot is cheaper but fragile. Not rely on linear scaling: shared dependencies (DB, cache) may cap earlier.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the curve convex? -> Queueing delay is proportional to utilisation divided by (1 - utilisation).
  • Would more threads per pod help? -> Not for CPU-bound work; it increases switches.
  • What about load shedding? -> Rejecting early keeps accepted requests fast and avoids timeouts and retries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team provisioned for 100% CPU and still failed in the campaign's first minutes; retries at p99 timeouts amplified load by 40%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: linear extrapolation.
  • Hire: identifies the non-linear knee and plans for lower utilisation.
  • Strong hire: computes capacity from measured knee, adds N+1 and burst margin, validates by test, and plans shedding and autoscaling signals.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem for a 25-minute partial outage. A feature team, to "guarantee low latency", set their event-processing threads to SCHED_FIFO priority 50 via chrt in the startup script on shared 8-core hosts. A bug in a retry loop (no sleep on error) turned one thread into a busy loop. Timeline: 09:14 deploy; 09:20 SSH to the host became unresponsive; 09:23 other services on the host missed health checks; 09:26 monitoring agent silent. After some time the host recovered partially:

$ dmesg | tail
sched: RT throttling activated
$ cat /proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_runtime_us /proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_period_us
950000
1000000
$ top -H
  PID USER PR  NI  S %CPU COMMAND
 8821 app  -51  0  R 94.0 worker-3

Management asks: "How was one thread able to take down other services?"
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: causes, timeline lessons, and action items.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A bug in the retry loop; fix the bug." Misses the guardrail failures.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who approved RT priority? Were there cgroup RT limits? Was the host shared? Did monitoring run at a lower class?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Retro) Use a serial console or a reserved core and chrt -o -p 0 8821 or kill the thread; drain the host.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (contributing factors): (a) real-time class always beats normal tasks (CFS), so the spinner starved everything including sshd and monitoring; (b) shared host with no isolation; (c) no review/guardrail for RT settings; (d) missing sleep or backoff in the retry loop; (e) default RT throttle of 95% still leaves only 5% for everyone else on that core, and it takes time to activate.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce on a test host; read scheduler docs; check how chrt was applied (script), cgroup cpu.rt_runtime_us availability; check kernel logs timeline.
  5. Root cause: A strict-priority policy without aging lets an RT task starve all lower-class tasks. The kernel's RT throttling is a last-resort safety net, not a protection for latency of other services.
  6. Fix: Remove RT policy in the app. If RT is truly needed, use dedicated cores (isolcpus/cpuset), keep system services off them, limit RT runtime per cgroup, and add a watchdog. Fix the bug: exponential backoff with jitter.
  7. Prevention: Policy: RT classes only on dedicated, non-shared hosts and with approval; admission control (OPA/Gatekeeper) rejecting SYS_NICE capability; load tests with fault injection (error storms); alerts on RT throttling messages and per-thread CPU.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Banning RT entirely hurts legitimate audio/robotics uses; I would restrict by capability and node pools instead. Not blame the engineer; the platform allowed it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Kubernetes not allow this by default? -> Needs the SYS_NICE capability; containers drop it by default.
  • Would nice -20 have caused the same? -> No; normal-class weights are proportional, never starving others entirely.
  • How could the team get low latency without RT? -> Dedicated cores (static CPU manager), correct thread counts, avoid throttling, cpu.weight.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" chrt fix lived in a script for two years until a retry bug exposed it; the host needed a hard reboot.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the retry bug only.
  • Hire: explains RT starvation and removes RT priority.
  • Strong hire: lists systemic guardrails (capabilities, node pools, throttling, alerts) and blameless, owned action items.
